title: More practice · C2
desc: Extra exercises for each C2 unit.
intro: One topic for each part of the unit. Each practice brings ALL the exercises of the topic: first the ones you got wrong, then the new ones.

sets.title: needn't have vs. didn't need to vs. didn't have to
sets.intro: Needn't have + participle says the action happened and was unnecessary. Didn't need to and didn't have to are neutral about what actually happened.

watch.wrong: She needn't to come.
watch.right: She needn't come.
watch.why: Needn't is a modal verb and takes no to.

watch.wrong: I needn't have gone, so I stayed home.
watch.right: I didn't need to go, so I stayed home.
watch.why: Needn't have + participle means you did go.

watch.wrong: You mustn't pay; it's free.
watch.right: You needn't pay; it's free.
watch.why: Mustn't means forbidden; needn't means not necessary.

items.prompt: You brought flowers? You ___ have! (need)
items.explain: Needn't have + past participle is the polite reply to an unnecessary gift.

items.prompt: We took umbrellas, but it stayed dry all day. We ___ have bothered. (need)
items.explain: Needn't have + participle: it happened and it was unnecessary.

items.prompt: Tomorrow is Sunday, so you ___ get up early.
items.explain: For the future, use needn't + base or don't need to / don't have to.

items.prompt: In the end nobody asked for a receipt, so we ___ to keep it.
items.explain: Didn't need to / didn't have to are neutral about what happened.

items.prompt: ___ I say more? The evidence speaks for itself.
items.explain: Need is a modal here, used in a rhetorical question.

items.prompt: You ___ only ask and she will help you.
items.explain: With only, need works as a modal: You need only ask.

items.prompt: He didn't ___ to apologise; nobody was upset.
items.explain: Didn't need to / didn't have to + base verb.

items.prompt: She paid in cash, so there ___ no need for her to fill in the form.
items.explain: Past time: there was no need for her to…

items.prompt: You ___ have waited for me; I could have found the way alone. (need not)
items.explain: Need not have + participle: you waited, but it wasn't necessary.

items.prompt: It is not necessary to book. You ___ book in advance. (modal, negative)
items.explain: The modal needn't is followed by a bare infinitive.

items.prompt: He fixed the roof himself, though the landlord would have paid. He ___ have done it. (need)
items.explain: He did it, and it was unnecessary: needn't have done.

items.prompt: American speakers usually say 'She doesn't ___ to come' where British speakers say 'She needn't come.'
items.explain: Doesn't need to is the usual American equivalent.

items.prompt: I rang the bell three times, but the door was open. I ___.
items.explain: I rang, and it was unnecessary: needn't have rung.

items.prompt: Which sentence means that going is forbidden?
Which sentence is NOT correct?
items.explain: The modal needn't never takes to.

items.prompt: 'You needn't have!' is the classic reply when someone ___.
items.explain: It means thank you, but it wasn't necessary.

items.prompt: The firm gave us a lift, so we ___ a taxi. (We did not take one.)
items.explain: Didn't need to is neutral, so it fits when nothing was done.

items.prompt: Which form stresses the absence of external obligation?
items.explain: Didn't have to focuses on lack of obligation.

items.prompt: She needn't to worry about the results.
answers: She needn't worry about the results.
She doesn't need to worry about the results.
items.explain: Needn't is a modal: no to.

items.prompt: He needn't have came so early.
answers: He needn't have come so early.
items.explain: Needn't have takes the past participle: come.

items.prompt: You don't need have apologised.
items.explain: Use needn't have + participle, or didn't need to + base.

items.prompt: She needs not have bothered.
items.explain: The modal has no -s: she needn't / need not.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: You needn't have gone to so much trouble.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: There was no need for her to come.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: Need I say any more about it?
items.explain: Need as a modal in a question.

items.prompt: No hacía falta que vinieras tan temprano, pero viniste.
answers: You needn't have come so early.
You need not have come so early.
You didn't need to come so early.
You didn't have to come so early.
items.explain: Needn't have + participle shows it happened in vain.

items.prompt: No necesitas decírmelo ahora; puedes esperar.
answers: You needn't tell me now; you can wait.
You don't need to tell me now; you can wait.
You don't have to tell me now; you can wait.
items.explain: Present or future: needn't + base verb.

items.prompt: Compré el libro, pero la biblioteca lo tenía: no hacía falta comprarlo.
answers: I bought the book, but the library had it; I needn't have bought it.
I bought the book, but the library had it; I need not have bought it.
items.explain: Needn't have bought: it was bought and unnecessary.

sets.title: might well, may as well, could do worse than and the certainty scale
sets.intro: Modal expressions place your judgement on a scale from certain to impossible. Might well raises the probability; might as well suggests resignation; could do worse than recommends something gently.

watch.wrong: It is probable to rain.
watch.right: It is likely to rain. / It is probable that it will rain.
watch.why: Probable never takes to + verb.

watch.wrong: He mustn't be at home.
watch.right: He can't be at home.
watch.why: Use can't for negative deduction.

watch.wrong: We might well go; there is nothing else to do.
watch.right: We might as well go; there is nothing else to do.
watch.why: Might as well = no reason not to; might well = quite likely.

items.prompt: That pipe is very old. It ___ well burst this winter.
items.explain: May / might / could well = quite likely.

items.prompt: The bus has gone. We ___ as well walk.
items.explain: May / might as well = there is no reason not to.

items.prompt: You ___ do worse than ask your sister for advice.
items.explain: Could do worse than + verb is a mild way to recommend something.

items.prompt: We ___ as well have stayed in bed; the trip achieved nothing.
items.explain: Might as well have + participle: what we did was pointless.

items.prompt: She is the best candidate, so she is ___ to get the job.
items.explain: Is bound / sure / certain to = almost 100 per cent.

items.prompt: It is highly ___ that the plan will work; I'd say five per cent.
items.explain: Highly improbable / unlikely = very low probability.

items.prompt: He ___ possibly know the answer; he wasn't even there.
Look at the lights. Somebody ___ be at home.
I saw her ten minutes ago, so she ___ have left the building. (negative deduction)
items.explain: Negative deduction uses can't / couldn't, never mustn't.

items.prompt: The sky is dark and it's ___ to rain soon.
items.explain: Likely works in is likely to + base.

items.prompt: It is perfectly ___ that the fault lies in the wiring.
items.explain: After it's, probable takes a that-clause.

items.prompt: This path is ___ to flood after heavy rain. (prone to)
items.explain: Liable to = prone to, usually something negative.

items.prompt: There's an outside ___ that she will change her mind.
items.explain: An outside chance is a very small chance.

items.prompt: It might ___ work, so let's try it. (a small but real possibility)
items.explain: Might just = a small but real possibility.

items.prompt: He ___ well refuse the offer; he has done so before.
items.explain: Might well = it is quite likely.

items.prompt: The mistake may well ___ been deliberate.
items.explain: May well have + participle: very possibly it happened.

items.prompt: If prices rise, it stands to ___ that sales will fall.
items.explain: It stands to reason = it is logical.

items.prompt: Which sentence means 'there is no reason not to go'?
items.explain: Might as well expresses resigned acceptance.

items.prompt: Which expresses the highest certainty?
items.explain: Be bound to is close to 100 per cent.

items.prompt: 'He can't be at home' means ___.
options: I am sure he is not at home
he is not allowed to be at home
it is possible he is at home

items.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
items.explain: There is no 'probable to'; use likely to.

items.prompt: 'We might as well have stayed at home.' suggests that going out was ___.
items.explain: Might as well have: it made no difference.

items.prompt: Which is the weakest probability?
In 'The path is liable to flood', liable to means ___.
items.explain: Liable to + base = likely to happen, often negatively.

items.prompt: It's probable to be cancelled.
answers: It's probable that it will be cancelled.
It is likely to be cancelled.
It is probable that it will be cancelled.
items.explain: Probable needs a that-clause; likely takes to.

items.prompt: She might as well to leave now.
answers: She might as well leave now.
items.explain: Might as well is followed by a bare infinitive.

items.prompt: He mustn't be at home; the lights are off.
answers: He can't be at home; the lights are off.
He couldn't be at home; the lights are off.
items.explain: Negative deduction needs can't, not mustn't.

items.prompt: You could to do worse than ask her.
answers: You could do worse than ask her.
items.explain: After a modal, use the bare infinitive.

items.prompt: They might well to have forgotten.
items.explain: Modal + well + have + participle; no to.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: We might as well wait for the next train.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: The mistake may well have been deliberate.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: There is an outside chance that she will agree.
items.explain: An outside chance = a very small chance.

items.prompt: Es muy probable que el director renuncie.
answers: The director is likely to resign.
The director is very likely to resign.
items.explain: Might / may well + base = quite likely.

items.prompt: Ya que estamos aquí, mejor entramos.
answers: We might as well go in.
We may as well go in.
Since we're here, we might as well go in.
As we're here, we might as well go in.
items.explain: Might as well suggests no reason not to.

items.prompt: Es imposible que lo sepa.
items.explain: Can't possibly = it is almost impossible.

items.prompt: Podrías hacer algo peor que aceptar su oferta.
answers: You could do worse than accept her offer.
You could do worse than accept his offer.
You could do worse than accepting her offer.
You could do worse than accepting his offer.
items.explain: Could do worse than = it would be a good idea.

sets.title: Stance adverbs
sets.intro: Stance adverbs modify the whole sentence and show the speaker's attitude: admittedly, ostensibly, arguably, tellingly. Beware of false friends such as eventually and actually.

watch.wrong: Actually, the company is hiring staff right now.
watch.right: Currently, the company is hiring staff right now.
watch.why: Actually does not mean 'currently'.

watch.wrong: Eventually it could be a mistake.
watch.right: Conceivably it could be a mistake.
watch.why: Eventually means 'in the end'.

watch.wrong: Enough curiously, nobody came.
watch.right: Curiously enough, nobody came.
watch.why: The order is adverb + enough.

items.prompt: ___, the plan has flaws, but it is still our best option. (I concede a weak point)
items.explain: Admittedly concedes a weak point before continuing.

items.prompt: The meeting was ___ held to discuss safety, but everyone knew it was about layoffs. (the official reason)
items.explain: Ostensibly hints that the official reason is false.

items.prompt: The suspect was ___ seen leaving the building at midnight, but the police have no footage. (reported without proof)
items.explain: Allegedly: someone claims it without proof.

items.prompt: Her argument is ___ absurd; no serious economist would accept it. (obviously, with disapproval)
This is ___ the finest novel of the decade, though some critics disagree. (it can be argued)
items.explain: Arguably = it can be argued that.

items.prompt: He is late again. ___, he missed the bus. (I suppose)
Curiously ___, nobody complained about the delay.
items.explain: Curiously enough = it is odd that.

items.prompt: We tried three methods and ___ found one that worked. (in the end)
items.explain: Eventually = in the end, after some time.

items.prompt: The firm is ___ hiring new staff. (at the present time)
items.explain: Currently = at present; actually does not mean this.

items.prompt: ___, everyone knew he would lose; the result was easy to predict.
___, no one was injured in the fire. (the speaker feels relief)
The chairman is ___ in charge, but his deputy makes every decision. (in name only)
___, she never once mentioned her team in the whole speech. (which is very revealing)
There is ___ no better cook in the village. (it cannot be denied)
He ___ resigned for health reasons, but the real cause was a quarrel. (the official reason)
___, the company went bankrupt a year after its record profits. (the speaker sees the irony)
items.explain: Ironically comments on an unexpected contrast.

items.prompt: 'Allegedly' suggests that the claim is ___.
Which adverb means 'which is very revealing'?
items.explain: Tellingly highlights something that reveals the truth.

items.prompt: 'Eventually' means ___.
items.explain: Eventually is a false friend of Spanish eventualmente.

items.prompt: Spanish 'actualmente' corresponds to ___.
Which adverb introduces a concession against your own position?
'Arguably' means ___.
'Ostensibly' hints that the official reason is ___.
items.explain: Ostensibly suggests a gap between appearance and reality.

items.prompt: Spanish 'eventualmente' (= posiblemente) is closest to ___.
Enough curiously, the door was unlocked.
answers: Curiously enough, the door was unlocked.

items.prompt: He is ostensible the owner, but his wife runs everything.
answers: He is ostensibly the owner, but his wife runs everything.

items.prompt: The result was patent absurd.
items.explain: An adverb is needed before an adjective: patently absurd.

items.prompt: Eventually it might rain tomorrow, so take a coat.
answers: Possibly it might rain tomorrow, so take a coat.
Conceivably it might rain tomorrow, so take a coat.
It might possibly rain tomorrow, so take a coat.

items.prompt: Supposedly to be a luxury hotel, it had no hot water.
answers: Supposedly a luxury hotel, it had no hot water.
It was supposedly a luxury hotel, but it had no hot water.
items.explain: Supposedly modifies the noun phrase, without to be.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: Admittedly, the film is far too long.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
Put the words in order.
answers: Tellingly, he never mentioned his brother.

items.prompt: Posiblemente la reunión se cancele.
answers: Conceivably the meeting will be cancelled.
The meeting might possibly be cancelled.
The meeting may possibly be cancelled.
Possibly the meeting will be cancelled.
items.explain: Conceivably / possibly express a mild probability.

items.prompt: Es indiscutiblemente la mejor solución.
answers: It is undeniably the best solution.
It is unquestionably the best solution.
It is indisputably the best solution.
items.explain: Undeniably = in a way that cannot be denied.

items.prompt: Supuestamente, es un experto, pero no sabe nada de leyes.
answers: Supposedly, he is an expert, but he knows nothing about law.
Supposedly he's an expert, but he knows nothing about law.

items.prompt: Actualmente trabajo en una editorial.
answers: I am currently working at a publishing house.
I currently work at a publishing house.
I'm currently working for a publishing house.
I currently work for a publisher.

sets.title: Reporting verbs with nuance
sets.intro: Reporting verbs do more than say who spoke: they show how sure, formal or doubtful the speaker is. Learn the nuance of each one.

learn.def: to say something is true without proof
learn.example: The seller claims the watch is a genuine antique.

learn.def: to state something firmly and confidently
learn.example: He asserted his right to speak at the meeting.

learn.def: to argue that something is true in a debate
learn.example: Critics contend that the policy favours the rich.

learn.def: to keep saying something is true despite doubt
learn.example: The driver maintained that the light was green.

learn.def: to say that someone did wrong, without proving it
learn.example: The report alleges that funds were misused.

learn.def: to demand or say something very firmly
learn.example: She insisted that we stay for dinner.

learn.def: to admit that something is true, usually unwillingly
learn.example: I concede that the first draft was weak.

learn.def: to state as a required condition
learn.example: The lease stipulates that pets are not allowed.

learn.def: to put forward as a starting point for argument
learn.example: Let us posit that the market will not recover.

learn.def: to claim openly, often with doubtful sincerity
learn.example: He professed great admiration for his rival.

items.prompt: The contract ___ that payment be made within thirty days. (sets as a condition)
items.explain: Stipulate = to fix as a condition.

items.prompt: The newspaper ___ that the minister took bribes, but it has no proof. (legal/press word)
items.explain: Allege = say someone did wrong without proving it.

items.prompt: Despite the evidence, he ___ that he had never met her. (kept saying the same thing)
items.explain: Maintain / insist = keep to a statement despite doubt.

items.prompt: Some philosophers ___ that free will is an illusion. (a reasoned argument)
items.explain: Contend = argue a position in a debate.

items.prompt: 'I am innocent,' he ___ firmly.
She ___ to have no interest in money, though she checks her accounts hourly. (claims, with doubt)
items.explain: Profess = claim, often with doubtful sincerity.

items.prompt: The document ___ to be an original, but it is clearly a copy.
items.explain: Purport to be = appear to be, with doubt.

items.prompt: I'll ___ that the idea has some merit, but I still disagree. (admit reluctantly)
Let us ___ for the sake of argument that the figures are correct. (set as a starting point)
items.explain: Posit = put forward as a premise.

items.prompt: The defence counsel ___ that the evidence was inadmissible. (respectfully put forward)
items.explain: Submit that is typical of courtroom language.

items.prompt: He openly ___ his loyalty to the cause. (formal, literary)
She would not back down; she ___ on seeing the manager.
'Allege' is typical of ___.
items.explain: Allege appears in the press and in law.

items.prompt: Which verb suggests the speaker doubts the claim?
items.explain: Purport to be = claim to be, but doubtful.

items.prompt: Which verb means 'to accept something unwillingly'?
Which verb best fits a calm, reasoned argument in a debate?
'The rule stipulates that…' means the rule ___.
'She maintained her innocence' means she ___.
He insisted me to apologise.
answers: He insisted that I should apologise.
items.explain: Insist takes a that-clause or on + -ing, not an object + to.

items.prompt: The report purports being impartial.
answers: The report purports to be impartial.
items.explain: Purport is followed by to + infinitive.

items.prompt: They alleged me of fraud.
answers: They alleged that I had committed fraud.
They alleged I had committed fraud.
items.explain: Allege takes a that-clause; accuse someone of.

items.prompt: He conceded me that he was wrong.
answers: He conceded to me that he was wrong.
He conceded that he was wrong.
items.explain: Concede that…, or concede to someone that…

items.prompt: The agreement stipulates for payment in advance.
answers: The agreement stipulates payment in advance.
items.explain: Stipulate is a transitive verb; no for.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: He has always maintained that he was misquoted.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: The prosecution alleges that the accused lied.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: Several scholars contend that the theory is flawed.

items.prompt: Él sostiene que nunca vio el documento.
answers: He maintains that he never saw the document.
He claims that he never saw the document.
He insists that he never saw the document.
He insists he never saw the document.
He maintains he never saw the document.
items.explain: Maintain = keep saying something is true.

items.prompt: La acusación alega que el contrato era falso.
answers: The prosecution alleges that the contract was false.
The prosecution alleges that the contract was fake.
The prosecution alleges that the contract was forged.

items.prompt: Reconozco a regañadientes que tienes razón.
answers: I reluctantly concede that you are right.
I concede, reluctantly, that you are right.
I reluctantly concede that you're right.

items.prompt: El contrato estipula que el pago debe hacerse en dólares.
answers: The contract stipulates that payment must be made in dollars.
The contract stipulates that payment should be made in dollars.
The contract stipulates that payment is to be made in dollars.

sets.title: Connotation: same referent, different judgement
sets.intro: Words with the same basic meaning can praise or criticise. Choosing a word shows your judgement, so learn the scale of each group.

learn.def: praise / neutral-positive / insult
learn.example: My neighbour is frugal, never stingy; he just hates waste.

learn.def: compliment / sometimes rude / unhealthy
learn.example: The old actor looked gaunt after the long tour.

learn.def: positive / neutral / negative
learn.example: The inquisitive child opened every drawer.

learn.def: positive / informal negative / very negative
learn.example: He is confident, not cocky; he listens to others.

learn.def: positive / negative / very negative
learn.example: She was assertive in the meeting but never aggressive.

learn.def: positive / negative
learn.example: There was something childlike in her delight at the snow.

learn.def: positive / negative / very negative informal
learn.example: Her determined effort paid off; his stubborn refusal did not.

learn.def: neutral / positive / negative
learn.example: They sell affordable furniture that lasts.

learn.def: positive / negative / very negative
learn.example: A firm manager is respected; an inflexible one is feared.

learn.def: informal positive / positive / negative
learn.example: Our laid-back landlord never complains about noise.

items.prompt: My grandmother is very ___ ; she never wastes anything, and we admire her for it. (positive)
items.explain: Thrifty / frugal praise careful use of money.

items.prompt: He won't even leave a tip: he's just ___. (negative: unwilling to spend)
After months of illness he looked pale and ___. (unhealthily thin)
She is so ___ that she can wear anything. (compliment)
The neighbour is ___ ; she asks about everyone's private life. (negative)
items.explain: Nosy = too curious about other people's affairs.

items.prompt: The students were ___ about how the machine worked and asked many questions. (neutral)
He thinks he is the best in the team and tells everyone: he's rather ___. (informal, negative)
Her ___ style won the deal; she was firm without being rude. (positive)
items.explain: Assertive is positive: firm but respectful.

items.prompt: The salesman was so ___ that I left the shop without buying. (negative)
His sense of wonder at the sea is almost ___. (positive)
Stop sulking: that is a ___ way to behave. (negative)
Nothing could change his mind: he was completely ___. (very negative, informal)
The shirt is ___ but well made. (positive: reasonably priced)
The manager is so ___ that she never gives way, even on small points. (very negative)
My boss is very ___ ; she never panics and trusts her team. (informal, positive)
We say 'elderly' or '___ citizens' to be respectful.
items.explain: Senior citizens is a polite institutional phrase.

items.prompt: Which word is a compliment?
Which word is the most negative?
'Nosy' describes someone who ___.
options: is too curious about others' affairs

items.prompt: Which adjective is neutral-positive for an unusual person?
A product described as 'cheap' sounds ___.
Which pair names the same quality with opposite judgements?
items.explain: Confident is positive; cocky is negative.

items.prompt: 'She is assertive' means she ___.
options: states her views firmly and fairly

items.prompt: I wanted to compliment her, so I said she looked gaunt.
answers: I wanted to compliment her, so I said she looked slim.
I wanted to compliment her, so I said she looked slender.
items.explain: Gaunt is not a compliment; slim is.

items.prompt: The brochure describes the hotel as cheap, to attract guests who want quality.
answers: The brochure describes the hotel as affordable, to attract guests who want quality.
The brochure describes the hotel as inexpensive, to attract guests who want quality.

items.prompt: The teacher praised the child's childish sense of wonder.
answers: The teacher praised the child's childlike sense of wonder.
items.explain: Childlike is positive; childish is negative.

items.prompt: Our grandfather is so thrifty that he never gives anyone a present; it is quite embarrassing.
answers: Our grandfather is so stingy that he never gives anyone a present; it is quite embarrassing.
Our grandfather is so mean that he never gives anyone a present; it is quite embarrassing.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: He calls himself frugal, but his friends call him stingy.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: They described the flat as affordable rather than cheap.
items.explain: Affordable is positive; cheap is negative.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: It is a thin line between determined and stubborn.

items.prompt: Mi abuela es austera, no tacaña.
answers: My grandmother is frugal, not stingy.
My grandmother is thrifty, not stingy.
My grandmother is frugal, not mean.
items.explain: Frugal is positive; stingy is negative.

items.prompt: No es curioso, es entrometido.
answers: He is not curious; he is nosy.
She is not curious; she is nosy.

items.prompt: Prefiero decir que es firme, no que es rígido.
answers: I prefer to say that she is firm, not rigid.
I prefer to say that he is firm, not rigid.
items.explain: Firm is positive; rigid is negative.

items.prompt: Los vecinos creen que es excéntrico; otros dicen que es raro.
answers: The neighbours think he is eccentric; others say he is weird.
The neighbours think she is eccentric; others say she is weird.

sets.title: Formulas for qualifying and positioning yourself
sets.intro: These fixed phrases soften, qualify or position an opinion. Learn their exact form: small changes make them wrong.

learn.def: used to give an opinion modestly
learn.example: For what it's worth, I would take the earlier train.

learn.en: as far as I can tell
learn.def: based on the information I have
learn.example: As far as I can tell, the bridge is safe.

learn.def: in practical terms
learn.example: To all intents and purposes, the contract is void.

learn.def: partly but not completely
learn.example: Up to a point, I share your concern.

learn.def: on the whole
learn.example: By and large, the staff are very supportive.

learn.en: I wouldn't go so far as to say…
learn.def: used to avoid exaggerating
learn.example: I wouldn't go so far as to say he lied.

learn.def: used for a small, opposite or additional effect
learn.example: If anything, the new rule has made queues longer.

learn.def: after weighing everything
learn.example: On balance, I would rather rent than buy.

learn.def: used for a strong understatement
learn.example: The service was, to put it mildly, slow.

learn.def: used to add a contrast
learn.example: Mind you, she had never driven before.

items.prompt: For what it's ___, I think the plan is sound.
items.explain: For what it's worth = for whatever my view is worth.

items.prompt: As far as I can ___, the printer is working again.
items.explain: As far as I can tell = based on what I know.

items.prompt: To all ___ and purposes, the project is finished.
items.explain: To all intents and purposes = in practical terms.

items.prompt: Up to a ___, she is right, but she ignores the costs.
___ and large, the residents are happy with the new park.
items.explain: By and large = on the whole.

items.prompt: I wouldn't go so ___ as to call it a disaster.
items.explain: I wouldn't go so far as to say = I wouldn't exaggerate.

items.prompt: The new schedule didn't help; if ___, it made things worse.
items.explain: If anything introduces a stronger, opposite possibility.

items.prompt: On ___, I would say the trip was worth the cost.
